title: When the Outcome Is Uncertain: How Competition and Expectation Errors Increase Cheating
abstract: ABSTRACT Why do individuals cheat in some situations but refrain from doing so in others? Existing research has primarily explained dishonest behavior in terms of achievement motivation, performance pressure, and expected payoffs, with less attention to how the predictability of behavioral outcomes shapes cheating decisions. Across four experiments, the present research examined the effects of competition, performance proximity, and outcome expectation accuracy on cheating and proposed a unified framework centered on outcome ambiguity. Study 1 showed that competition increased cheating magnitude relative to a noncompetitive context. Study 2 further demonstrated that cheating increased when competitors' performance was closer and the final outcome was therefore more difficult to predict. Studies 3 and 4 extended this pattern beyond competitive contexts, showing that inaccurate outcome expectations increased cheating magnitude, whereas accurate expectations reduced it. Taken together, these findings suggest that competition, close competitive outcomes, and inaccurate outcome expectations, although distinct situational factors, may share a common feature: they reduce the predictability of final outcomes and make it less clear whether and how one's actions will influence those outcomes. Such outcome ambiguity, in turn, may increase cheating magnitude. These findings suggest that cheating is driven not only by the pursuit of favorable outcomes but also by uncertainty regarding the relationship between one's actions and their consequences. Drawing on compensatory control theory, we further propose that when individuals have difficulty predicting or controlling final outcomes, cheating may serve as a compensatory strategy for regaining a sense of control over those outcomes. The present research extends behavioral decision research on dishonesty by highlighting outcome predictability and perceived controllability as potentially important determinants of cheating decisions.
